modern_osis:
Nehemiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The Old Testament's historical narrative closes with the book of Nehemiah.

It records how Nehemiah's heart responded as he managed public affairs, along with many devout reflections.

Original heading

Nehemiah's distress for the misery of Jerusalem, His prayer.

Nehemiah's concern and prayer

Nehemiah served as cupbearer to the Persian king. When God has work to accomplish, he will always have suitable people to do it.

Nehemiah lived comfortably and held an honored position. Nevertheless, he remembered that he was an Israelite and that his fellow Israelites were suffering.

He was ready to help them in every way he could. To find out how best to help, he asked about their condition. We should take a special interest in the condition of God's church and the state of religion.

Every earthly Jerusalem has shortcomings that need the support and service of its friends. Only the heavenly Jerusalem is without defect.

Nehemiah went first to God in prayer so that he could approach the king with greater confidence. Our strongest arguments in prayer come from God's own promises—the word on which he has taught us to hope.

We must also use the practical means available to us, but the earnest and effective prayer of a righteous person accomplishes much. Fellowship with God best prepares us for dealing with other people.

After we have entrusted a concern to God, our minds are set free. We gain contentment and composure, and our difficulties no longer seem insurmountable.

We know that if what we seek would harm us, God can readily prevent it; and if it would be good for us, he can just as readily bring it about.
classic_reading:
[Neh.1.1]
Nehemiah
The Old Testament history closes with the book of Nehemiah, wherein is recorded the workings of his heart, in the management of public affairs; with many devout reflections.
Chapter 1
Nehemiah's distress for the misery of Jerusalem, His prayer.
--Nehemiah was the Persian king's cup-bearer. When God has work to do, he will never want instruments to do it with. Nehemiah lived at ease, and in honour, but does not forget that he is an Israelite, and that his brethren are in distress. He was ready to do them all the good offices he could; and that he might know how best to do them a kindness, he makes inquiries about them. We should inquire especially concerning the state of the church and religion. Every Jerusalem on this side the heavenly one will have some defect, which will require the help and services of its friends. Nehemiah's first application was to God, that he might have the fuller confidence in his application to the king. Our best pleas in prayer are taken from the promise of God, the word on which he has caused us to hope. Other means must be used, but the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails most. Communion with God will best prepare us for our dealings with men. When we have intrusted our concerns to God, the mind is set at liberty; it feels satisfaction and composure, and difficulties vanish. We know that if the affair be hurtful, he can easily hinder it; and if it be good for us, he can as easily forward it.

Nehemiah asks the king (verses 1–8)

Our prayers must be accompanied by serious efforts; otherwise we are making a mockery of prayer.

We are not restricted to fixed times when approaching the King of kings. We may turn to him at any moment. It is never the wrong time to approach his throne of grace.

Yet God's displeasure and the suffering of his people cause sorrow to his children—a sorrow that no earthly pleasure can remove.

The king encouraged Nehemiah to explain what troubled him. This gave Nehemiah courage to speak.

How much greater courage should we take from Christ's invitation to pray and his promise that our prayers will be heard! We can approach the throne of grace with confidence.

Nehemiah prayed to the God of heaven, who is infinitely greater than the powerful earthly king standing before him.

He raised his heart to the God who understands the language of hearts.

We should never undertake anything for which it would be wrong to seek and expect God's guidance, help and blessing.

His prayer received an immediate answer: the descendants of Jacob have never sought the God of Jacob in vain.

Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem (verses 9–18)

After studying the situation, Nehemiah told the Jews that God had put it into his heart to rebuild Jerusalem's wall.

He did not intend to accomplish this work without them.

When we encourage ourselves and one another toward what is good, we strengthen one another to do it.

We perform our duties weakly when we are indifferent or careless.

Opposition to the work (verses 19 and 20)

The hostility of the serpent's offspring toward Christ's cause is not limited to any particular age or country.

The lesson for us is clear. God's church needs our help. Is it not exposed to attacks and sometimes left desolate?

Does its low condition grieve us?

We must not become so absorbed by business, amusement or support for a particular group that Zion and its welfare no longer matter to us.

Verses 1-8
Our prayers must be seconded with serious endeavours, else we mock God. We are not limited to certain moments in our addresses to the King of kings, but have liberty to go to him at all times; approaches to the throne of grace are never out of season. But the sense of God's displeasure and the afflictions of his people, are causes of sorrow to the children of God, under which no earthly delights can comfort. The king encouraged Nehemiah to tell his mind. This gave him boldness to speak; much more may the invitation Christ has given us to pray, and the promise that we shall speed, encourage us to come boldly to the throne of grace. Nehemiah prayed to the God of heaven, as infinitely above even this mighty monarch. He lifted up his heart to that God who understands the language of the heart. Nor should we ever engage in any pursuit in which it would be wrong for us thus to seek and expect the Divine direction, assistance, and blessing. There was an immediate answer to his prayer; for the seed of Jacob never sought the God of Jacob in vain.
[Neh.2.9-Neh.2.18]
Verses 9-18
When Nehemiah had considered the matter, he told the Jews that God had put it into his heart to build the wall of Jerusalem. He does not undertake to do it without them. By stirring up ourselves and one another to that which is good, we strengthen ourselves and one another for it. We are weak in our duty, when we are cold and careless.
[Neh.2.19-Neh.2.20]
Verses 19-20
The enmity of the serpent's seed against the cause of Christ is confined to no age or nation. The application to ourselves is plain. The church of God asks for our help. Is it not desolate, and exposed to assaults? Does the consideration of its low estate cause you any grief? Let not business, pleasure, or the support of a party so engage attention, as that Zion and her welfare shall be nothing to you.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem.

Rebuilding Jerusalem's walls

The work was divided so that everyone knew the particular task assigned to them and could attend to it with a desire to do it well.

They competed only in doing as much good as possible for the community, not in pursuing conflicting interests or quarrelling with one another.

Every Israelite should lend a hand in building up Jerusalem.

People in high positions should never consider a task beneath their dignity when it will benefit their country. Even some women joined in the work.

Some worked on sections opposite their own houses, and one worked opposite his room.

When a great common task needs doing, everyone should begin with the part within their own reach.

If everyone swept the space outside their own door, the whole street would be clean. If everyone repaired one part, the entire wall would be repaired.

Some who had finished their own assignments helped their neighbors finish theirs.

The broken walls and piles of debris around Jerusalem picture the desperate condition of the world around us.

The number and malice of the people hindering the construction give us some small idea of the enemies Christians meet while doing God's work.

Everyone must begin at home. By advancing God's work in our own souls, we can contribute most effectively to the good of Christ's church.

May the Lord stir up his people's hearts to set aside petty disputes and consider worldly interests insignificant compared with rebuilding Jerusalem's walls and defending truth and godliness against open enemies.
classic_reading:
[Neh.3.1]
Chapter 3
The rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem.
--The work was divided, so that every one might know what he had to do, and mind it, with a desire to excel; yet without contention, or separate interests. No strife appears among them, but which should do most for the public good. Every Israelite should lend a hand toward the building up of Jerusalem. Let not nobles think any thing below them, by which they may advance the good of their country. Even some females helped forward the work. Some repaired over against their houses, and one repaired over against his chamber. When a general good work is to be done, each should apply himself to that part which is within his reach. If every one will sweep before his own door, the street will be clean; if every one will mend one, we shall all be mended. Some that had first done helped their fellows. The walls of Jerusalem, in heaps of rubbish, represent the desperate state of the world around, while the number and malice of those who hindered the building, give some faint idea of the enemies we have to contend with, while executing the work of God. Every one must begin at home; for it is by getting the work of God advanced in our own souls that we shall best contribute to the good of the church of Christ. May the Lord thus stir up the hearts of his people, to lay aside their petty disputes, and to disregard their worldly interests, compared with building the walls of Jerusalem, and defending the cause of truth and godliness against the assaults of avowed enemies.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesOpposition of Sanballat and others.1–6The designs of the adversaries.7–15Nehemiah's precautions.16–23
Sanballat and others oppose the work (verses 1–6)

Proud and arrogant mockers have despised many a good work.

People who disagree about almost everything may nevertheless unite in persecution.

Nehemiah did not answer foolish insults in kind. He looked up to God in prayer.

God's people have often been despised, but the Lord hears every insult directed toward them. This knowledge comforts them.

Nehemiah had reason to believe these enemies had become desperately hardened in heart; otherwise he would not have prayed that their sins never be wiped away.

Good work progresses well when people have the heart to do it. Enemy insults should make us more diligent in duty, not drive us away from it.

The enemies plan to stop the building (verses 7–15)

Wicked people aim to obstruct good work and expect their plans to succeed. But work done for God is his work, and it will prosper.

God can expose and defeat the plans of his church's enemies in many ways.

If our enemies cannot frighten us away from duty or deceive us into sin, they cannot truly hurt us.

Nehemiah entrusted himself and his cause to God's protection, as we should.

He laid all his cares, sorrows and fears before God.

He prayed before taking practical measures. Then, after praying, he appointed a guard.

If we expect prayer to protect us without vigilance, we are lazy and put God to the test.

If we depend on vigilance without prayer, we are proud and disregard God.

Either way, we abandon the path of his protection.

God's care for our safety should encourage us to perform our duties vigorously.

Once the danger has passed, let us return to work and trust him when new trouble comes.

Nehemiah's precautions (verses 16–23)

We must remain watchful against spiritual enemies and not imagine that the struggle ends before our work is finished.

The word of God is the sword of the Spirit.

It should always be within reach, so that we never have to search for it when we are working or fighting as Christians.

Every true Christian is both a worker and a soldier, building with one hand and fighting with the other.

Good work progresses when those doing it treat it seriously.

Satan fears the watchful Christian. If he does attack, the Lord fights for his servant.

We must continue until the end of life, never putting aside our armor until our work and warfare have finished.

Then we will be welcomed into our Lord's rest and joy.

Verses 1-6
Many a good work has been looked upon with contempt by proud and haughty scorners. Those who disagree in almost every thing, will unite in persecution. Nehemiah did not answer these fools according to their folly, but looked up to God by prayer. God's people have often been a despised people, but he hears all the slights that are put upon them, and it is their comfort that he does so. Nehemiah had reason to think that the hearts of those sinners were desperately hardened, else he would not have prayed that their sins might never be blotted out. Good work goes on well, when people have a mind to it. The reproaches of enemies should quicken us to our duty, not drive us from it.
[Neh.4.7-Neh.4.15]
Verses 7-15
The hindering good work is what bad men aim at, and promise themselves success in; but good work is God's work, and it shall prosper. God has many ways of bringing to light, and so of bringing to nought, the devices and designs of his church's enemies. If our enemies cannot frighten us from duty, or deceive us into sin, they cannot hurt us. Nehemiah put himself and his cause under the Divine protection. It was the way of this good man, and should be our way. All his cares, all his griefs, all his fears, he spread before God. Before he used any means, he made his prayer to God. Having prayed, he set a watch against the enemy. If we think to secure ourselves by prayer, without watchfulness, we are slothful, and tempt God; if by watchfulness, without prayer, we are proud, and slight God: either way, we forfeit his protection. God's care of our safety, should engage and encourage us to go on with vigour in our duty. As soon as a danger is over, let us return to our work, and trust God another time.
[Neh.4.16-Neh.4.23]
Verses 16-23
We must watch always against spiritual enemies, and not expect that our warfare will be over till our work is ended. The word of God is the sword of the Spirit, which we ought to have always at hand, and never to have to seek for it, either in our labours, or in our conflicts, as Christians. Every true Christian is both a labourer and a soldier, working with one hand, and fighting with the other. Good work is likely to go on with success, when those who labour in it, make a business of it. And Satan fears to assault the watchful Christian; or, if attacked, the Lord fights for him. Thus must we wait to the close of life, never putting off our armour till our work and warfare are ended; then we shall be welcomed to the rest and joy of our Lord.

The people's grievances (verses 1–5)

People exploit one another. Those who despise the poor insult their Creator.

This is disgraceful conduct for anyone, but especially hateful when practiced by people who profess to be Christians.

We should sympathize with oppressed people and grieve over the hardships under which so many suffer.

We ought to put ourselves in their place, remembering them both in prayer and through practical help.

People who show no mercy must expect judgment without mercy.

Nehemiah confronts the abuses (verses 6–13)

Nehemiah knew that however high, thick or strong he built Jerusalem's walls, the city would remain insecure while injustice continued inside.

The right way to reform people's conduct is to convince their consciences.

Those who truly fear God will not covet worldly wealth or treat brothers and sisters cruelly.

Nothing brings more disgrace upon religion than worldliness and hardheartedness in those who claim to practice it.

People who insist harshly on every one of their own rights can scarcely persuade others to give up theirs.

When reasoning with selfish people, it is helpful to contrast their conduct with the generosity of others.

But the greatest example is Christ, who was rich and became poor for us, so that through his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The people did what they had promised.

Good promises are valuable, but doing what was promised is better.

Nehemiah's restraint as governor (verses 14–19)

Those who truly fear God will not dare to act cruelly or unjustly.

Everyone holding public office should remember that its purpose is to do good, not to enrich the officeholder.

Nehemiah asked God in prayer to remember his service.

He was not claiming to have earned favor from God.

Instead, he trusted God to make up for what he had spent or sacrificed for God's honor.

He spoke and acted as a person conscious of his own sin.

He did not demand a reward as a debt owed to him.

He looked to the Lord who graciously rewards even a cup of cold water given to a disciple for Christ's sake.

Fear and love of God, together with true love for brothers and sisters, lead to every good work.

These works are proper evidence of justifying faith, not the price paid to obtain it.

Our reconciled God regards such people for good according to their service for his people.

Verses 1-5
Men prey upon their fellow-creatures: by despising the poor they reproach their Maker. Such conduct is a disgrace to any, but who can sufficiently abhor it when adopted by professing Christians? With compassion for the oppressed, we should lament the hardships which many in the world are groaning under; putting our souls into their souls' stead, and remembering in our prayers and succours those who are burdened. But let those who show no mercy, expect judgment without mercy.
[Neh.5.6-Neh.5.13]
Verses 6-13
Nehemiah knew that, if he built Jerusalem's walls ever so high, so thick, or so strong, the city could not be safe while there were abuses. The right way to reform men's lives, is to convince their consciences. If you walk in the fear of God, you will not be either covetous of worldly gain, or cruel toward your brethren. Nothing exposes religion more to reproach, than the worldliness and hard-heartedness of the professors of it. Those that rigorously insist upon their right, with a very ill grace try to persuade others to give up theirs. In reasoning with selfish people, it is good to contrast their conduct with that of others who are liberal; but it is best to point to His example, who though he was rich, yet for our sakes became poor, that we, through his poverty, might be rich, [2Cor.8.9] 2Co 8:9. They did according to promise. Good promises are good things, but good performances are better.
[Neh.5.14-Neh.5.19]
Verses 14-19
Those who truly fear God, will not dare to do any thing cruel or unjust. Let all who are in public places remember that they are so placed to do good, not to enrich themselves. Nehemiah mentions it to God in prayer, not as if he had merited any favour from God, but to show that he depended upon God only, to make up to him what he had lost and laid out for his honour. Nehemiah evidently spake and acted as one that knew himself to be a sinner. He did not mean to claim a reward as of debt, but in the manner that the Lord rewards a cup of cold water given to a disciple for his sake. The fear and love of God in the heart, and true love of the brethren, will lead to every good work. These are proper evidences of justifying faith; and our reconciled God will look upon persons of this character for good, according to all they have done for his people.

Sanballat plots to hinder Nehemiah (verses 1–9)

When worthless companions try to lure us into idle, amusing gatherings, we can answer: We have work to do, and we must not neglect it.

We must never allow repeated pressure to wear us down into doing something sinful or unwise. When the same temptation returns, we must resist with the same reasons and determination.

Malicious people often claim that everyone wants something when in reality only they want it.

Nehemiah understood their intention. He denied not only the charges against him but also the claim that such rumors were being circulated.

His reputation was too well established for the accusations to be credible.

We should never abandon a known duty for fear that others may misunderstand it. Instead, maintain a good conscience and entrust your reputation to God.

Even when God's people are widely insulted, their good name may be far stronger than their opponents suggest.

Nehemiah sent up a brief prayer to heaven.

Whenever Christians face a task or a spiritual conflict, they may pray: God, strengthen my hands for the work and the temptation before me.

Every attempt to distract us from our duty should make us more determined to perform it.

False prophets attempt to frighten Nehemiah (verses 10–14)

The worst harm enemies can do to us is to frighten us away from good work or persuade us to sin.

Never abandon a good work; never do a bad one.

Test every piece of advice and reject whatever contradicts God's word.

All believers should pursue consistency with their calling.

Can I profess to be a Christian, a saint, God's child, a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit, yet still be greedy, sensual, proud, envious, impatient, discontented or angry?

Can I give in to laziness, unbelief or lack of mercy?

What influence will such behavior have on other people?

Everything God has done for us, given us or accomplished through us ought to make us vigilant, self-denying and diligent.

After sin's inherent evil, we should dread the scandal our sin brings upon God's cause.

The wall is completed despite betrayal (verses 15–19)

The wall was completed in fifty-two days, even though the workers rested on the Sabbaths.

Much can be accomplished in little time when people undertake a task sincerely and keep at it.

The alliances created through marriages with foreigners became harmful here.

Once people became relatives of Tobiah, they soon bound themselves to his cause.

Sinful affection can lead to sinful alliances.

The enemy of souls uses many agents and many schemes to disgrace active servants of God or draw them away from their service.

But we should follow the One who gave his life for the sheep.

Those who remain simply and faithfully devoted to the Lord and his work will receive his support.

Verses 1-9
Let those who are tempted to idle merry meetings by vain companions, thus answer the temptation, We have work to do, and must not neglect it. We must never suffer ourselves to be overcome, by repeated urgency, to do anything sinful or imprudent; but when attacked with the same temptation, must resist it with the same reason and resolution. It is common for that which is desired only by the malicious, to be falsely represented by them as desired by the many. But Nehemiah knew at what they aimed, he not only denied that such things were true, but that they were reported; he was better known than to be thus suspected. We must never omit any known duty for fear it should be misconstrued; but, while we keep a good conscience, let us trust God with our good name. God's people, though loaded with reproach, are not really fallen so low in reputation as some would have them thought to be. Nehemiah lifted up his heart to Heaven in a short prayer. When, in our Christian work and warfare, we enter upon any service or conflict, this is a good prayer, I have such a duty to do, such a temptation to grapple with; now, therefore, O God, strengthen my hands. Every temptation to draw us from duty, should quicken us the more to duty.
[Neh.6.10-Neh.6.14]
Verses 10-14
The greatest mischief our enemies can do us, is, to frighten us from our duty, and to lead us to do what is sinful. Let us never decline a good work, never do a bad one. We ought to try all advice, and to reject what is contrary to the word of God. Every man should study to be consistent. Should I, a professed Christian, called to be a saint, a child of God, a member of Christ, a temple of the Holy Ghost, should I be covetous, sensual, proud, or envious? Should I yield to impatience, discontent, or anger? Should I be slothful, unbelieving, or unmerciful? What effects will such conduct have upon others? All that God has done for us, or by us, or given to us, should lead us to watchfulness, self-denial, and diligence. Next to the sinfulness of sin, we should dread the scandal.
[Neh.6.15-Neh.6.19]
Verses 15-19
The wall was begun and finished in fifty-two days, though they rested on the sabbaths. A great deal of work may be done in a little time, if we set about it in earnest, and keep close to it. See the mischief of marrying with strangers. When men once became akin to Tobiah, they soon became sworn to him. A sinful love leads to a sinful league. The enemy of souls employs many instruments, and forms many projects, to bring reproach on the active servants of God, or to take them from their work. But we should follow the example of Him who laid down his life for the sheep. Those that simply cleave to the Lord and his work will be supported.

Jerusalem is entrusted to Hananiah (verses 1–4)

After completing the wall, Nehemiah returned to the Persian court.

He later came back to Jerusalem under a new commission.

Public safety depends in part upon every person's care to guard themselves and their households against sin.

The list of those who first returned (verses 5–73)

Nehemiah knew that, under God, a city's safety depends more on the character of its inhabitants than on the strength of its walls.

Every good gift and good work comes from heaven.

God grants both knowledge and grace. Everything comes from him, so everything should be devoted to him.

When human foresight produces good results, we must acknowledge the direction of divine Providence.

How terrible for those who turn away from the Lord because they love the present world!

How happy those who dedicate themselves and their possessions to God's service and glory!

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe reading and expounding the law.1–8The people called upon to be joyful.9–12The feast of tabernacles, The joy of the people.13–18
The law is read and explained (verses 1–8)

Sacrifices had to be offered at the entrance of the temple.

Prayer and preaching, however, could be carried out acceptably in many different places, both then and now.

Household leaders should bring their families to public worship.

Women and children have souls that need salvation. They therefore need to know God's word and attend the means of grace.

Young children should be taught religion as soon as they become capable of understanding it.

Ministers should take their Bibles into the pulpit, as Ezra did.

Scripture must be the source of their knowledge and the standard for everything they teach.

Reading Scripture aloud in a gathered congregation is an ordinance God has appointed to honor himself and build up his church.

Listeners need to understand what they hear. Otherwise it is only an empty sequence of words.

Teachers must therefore explain the text and make its meaning clear.

Reading is valuable and preaching is valuable. But explaining the meaning of Scripture helps people understand what is read and makes preaching more convincing.

In almost every age God has raised up preachers and also writers who explain biblical truth.

Some commentators have made matters darker through ignorant words, but the work of others has been extremely useful.

Nevertheless, every teaching must be tested by Scripture.

The people listened eagerly and paid attention to every word.

God's word deserves our close attention. If carelessness makes us miss much while listening, forgetfulness may cause us to lose everything afterward.

The people are told to rejoice (verses 9–12)

The people's tears when they heard God's law showed that their hearts had become tender.

They were told to send food to those who had nothing prepared.

Both a solemn feast and a solemn fast should move us to compassion for hungry people.

God's generosity should make us generous, not only to people who come asking but also to those we must actively seek out.

Their strength lay in joy in the Lord.

The more deeply we understand God's word, the greater comfort we find in it.

Much of the darkness we experience in trouble comes from ignorance.

The Feast of Tabernacles (verses 13–18)

Through careful study, the people rediscovered the law concerning the Feast of Tabernacles.

People who diligently search Scripture often find instructions they had forgotten.

The feast pictured the believer's temporary dwelling in this world and the holy joy of the gospel church.

Zechariah's prophecy pictures the nations coming to faith in Christ through this feast (Zechariah 14:16).

True religion makes us recognize ourselves as strangers and pilgrims on earth.

We read and hear God's word rightly when we do what it commands, including renewing duties long neglected.

The people observed the reality signified by the ceremony. Without that, the outward rite would have been useless.

They obeyed while rejoicing in God and his goodness.

These are the appointed means through which the Holy Spirit brings sinners to reverence, repentance and humility before God.

But those who continually indulge sorrow—even sorrow for sin—and refuse the comfort offered through God's word and Spirit become enemies of their own growth in holiness.

Verses 1-8
Sacrifices were to be offered only at the door of the temple; but praying and preaching were, and are, services of religion, as acceptably performed in one place as in another. Masters of families should bring their families with them to the public worship of God. Women and children have souls to save, and are therefore to acquaint themselves with the word of God, and to attend on the means of grace. Little ones, as they come to reason, must be trained up in religion. Ministers when they go to the pulpit, should take their Bibles with them; Ezra did so. Thence they must fetch their knowledge; according to that rule they must speak, and must show that they do so. Reading the Scriptures in religious assemblies is an ordinance of God, whereby he is honoured, and his church edified. Those who hear the word, should understand it, else it is to them but an empty sound of words. It is therefore required of teachers that they explain the word, and give the sense of it. Reading is good, and preaching is good, but expounding makes reading the better understood, and preaching the more convincing. It has pleased God in almost every age of the church to raise up, not only those who have preached the gospel, but also those who have given their views of Divine truth in writing; and though many who have attempted to explain Scripture, have darkened counsel by words without knowledge, yet the labours of others are of excellent use. All that we hear must, however, be brought to the test of Scripture. They heard readily, and minded every word. The word of God demands attention. If through carelessness we let much slip in hearing, there is danger that through forgetfulness we shall let all slip after hearing.
[Neh.8.9-Neh.8.12]
Verses 9-12
It was a good sign that their hearts were tender, when they heard the words of the law. The people were to send portions to those for whom nothing was prepared. It is the duty of a religious feast, as well as of a religious fast, to draw out the soul to the hungry; God's bounty should make us bountiful. We must not only give to those that offer themselves, but send to those out of sight. Their strength consisted in joy in the Lord. The better we understand God's word, the more comfort we find in it; the darkness of trouble arises from the darkness of ignorance.
[Neh.8.13-Neh.8.18]
Verses 13-18
They found written in the law about the feast of tabernacles. Those who diligently search the Scriptures, find things written there which they have forgotten. This feast of tabernacles was a representation of the believer's tabernacle state in this world, and a type of the holy joy of the gospel church. The conversion of the nations to the faith of Christ, is foretold under the figure of this feast, [Zech.14.16] Zec 14:16. True religion will render us strangers and pilgrims upon earth. We read and hear the word acceptably and profitably, when we do according to what is written therein; when what appears to be our duty is revived, after it has been neglected. They minded the substance; else the ceremony had been of no use. They did it, rejoicing in God and his goodness. These are the means which the Spirit of God crowns with success, in bringing the hearts of sinners to tremble and to become humbled before God. But those are enemies to their own growth in holiness, who always indulge sorrow, even for sin, and put away from them the consolations tendered by the word and Spirit of God.

The people fast and read God's word (verses 1–3)

Scripture directs and strengthens our prayers because the Spirit uses it to help us in our weakness.

Careful study of God's word increasingly shows us our sinfulness and the abundance of his salvation.

It calls us both to mourn our sin and to rejoice in him.

Every new discovery of divine truth should make us more diligent, not less diligent, in hearing God's word and taking part in his worship.

Prayer, history and confession (verses 4–38)

Scripture preserves a summary of the prayers offered on this occasion. Undoubtedly much more was said.

Whatever ability God gives us for our duties should be used as fully as possible for his glory.

When confessing sin, it is good to remember God's mercies. His generosity makes our ingratitude more evident and deepens our humility and shame.

The Lord's treatment of Israel displayed his goodness and patience alongside the stubbornness of the people's hearts.

The prophets' testimony was the Spirit's testimony through them—the Spirit of Christ speaking through the prophets.

They spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, so their words must be received accordingly.

The account moved the people to wonder at God's mercy and to recognize that their sins had brought them into their present condition.

Only unearned love could deliver them.

Is their history not a picture of our common human nature?

Let us examine our nation's history and our own lives.

Recall the advantages we had from childhood and ask how we first responded to them.

Do this often so we may remain humble, grateful and alert.

Pride and stubborn resistance to God destroy the soul.

Yet sometimes it is just as difficult to persuade a brokenhearted sinner to hope as it once was to persuade that sinner to fear.

Are you in that condition?

Consider the wonderful promise that God is ready to forgive.

Do not stay away from him because you feel unworthy.

Come boldly to his throne of grace, where mercy and timely help can be found.

He is ready to forgive.

The word will direct and quicken prayer, for by it the Spirit helps our infirmities in prayer. The careful study of God's word will more and more discover to us our own sinfulness, and the plenteousness of his salvation; thus it calls us to mourn for sin, and to rejoice in him. Every discovery of the truth of God, should render us more unwearied in attendance on his sacred word, and on his worship.
[Neh.9.4-Neh.9.38]
Verses 4-38
The summary of their prayers we have here upon record. Much more, no doubt, was said. Whatever ability we have to do any thing in the way of duty, we are to serve and glorify God according to the utmost of it. When confessing our sins, it is good to notice the mercies of God, that we may be the more humbled and ashamed. The dealings of the Lord showed his goodness and long-suffering, and the hardness of their hearts. The testimony of the prophets was the testimony of the Spirit in the prophets, and it was the Spirit of Christ in them. They spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost, and what they said is to be received accordingly. The result was, wonder at the Lord's mercies, and the feeling that sin had brought them to their present state, from which nothing but unmerited love could rescue them. And is not their conduct a specimen of human nature? Let us study the history of our land, and our own history. Let us recollect our advantages from childhood, and ask what were our first returns? Let us frequently do so, that we may be kept humble, thankful, and watchful. Let all remember that pride and obstinacy are sins which ruin the soul. But it is often as hard to persuade the broken-hearted to hope, as formerly it was to bring them to fear. Is this thy case? Behold this sweet promise, A God ready to pardon! Instead of keeping away from God under a sense of unworthiness, let us come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. He is a God ready to pardon.

The covenant is signed (verses 1–31)

Conversion means separating from the ways and habits of this world and devoting ourselves to the conduct commanded in God's word.

When we bind ourselves to obey God's commands, we undertake to obey all of them.

We also acknowledge that he is not only the Lord in a general sense, but our Lord.

The people undertake renewed worship (verses 32–39)

Having made a covenant against the sins they had committed, the people now undertook the duties they had neglected.

We must do more than stop doing evil: we must learn to do good.

No community should expect God's blessing while allowing public worship to fall into neglect.

Families are more likely to prosper when God's house and its work are properly supported.

When everyone contributes, even if each individual gift is small, the combined contribution can be substantial.

We must do what we can in acts of devotion and charity.

Whatever our circumstances, we should joyfully carry out our duty to God. This is the surest path to freedom and contentment.

God's appointed ordinances nourish and strengthen believers' souls, so they should not resent the expense of supporting them.

Yet many people let their souls go hungry.

Verses 1-31
Conversion is separating from the course and custom of this world, devoting ourselves to the conduct directed by the word of God. When we bind ourselves to do the commandments of God, it is to do all his commandments, and to look to him as the Lord, and our Lord.
[Neh.10.32-Neh.10.39]
Verses 32-39
Having covenanted against the sins of which they had been guilty, they obliged themselves to observe the duties they had neglected. We must not only cease to do evil, but learn to do well. Let not any people expect the blessing of God, unless they keep up public worship. It is likely to go well with our houses, when care is taken that the work of God's house goes on well. When every one helps, and every one gives, though but little, toward a good work, the whole will come to be a large sum. We must do what we can in works of piety and charity; and whatever state we are placed in, cheerfully perform our duty to God, which will be the surest way to ease and liberty. As the ordinances of God are the appointed means of support to our souls, the believer will not grudge the expense; yet most people leave their souls to starve.
